Article Title: Asian Games: MMA's Varun Sanyal declared medically unfit in attempt at weight cut after getting dizzy in sauna
Article Text:
Varun Sanyal (Photo-X)

What did IOA say?

Who is Varun Sanyal?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New Delhi: India's MMA fighter in 77kg category, Varun Sanyal was ruled out of the Asian Games after being declared medically unfit for the competition at the weigh-in process. The athlete felt dizzy at a sauna for weight cut and passed out at the facility.“While undergoing weight loss, including food and fluid restriction, experienced dizziness, lightheadedness, and muscle cramps 30 minutes after taking a sauna,” said a document assessing his condition.He was reportedly tended to by a fellow athlete and MMA India president Nikhil Kunder. He was taken to a doctor and then declared medically unfit for competition.Varun is one of the two Indian MMA fighters in India's Asian Games squad and had a challenging integration at the continental competition. Like many other athletes, he had faced a challenging time with getting a room upon arrival in Japan.The other MMA fighter in the squad -- Suchika Tariyal -- won her quarter-final bout and confirmed a medal for India. She will next take part in the semi-finals of women’s 60kg event."Varun Sanyal suffered from generalized cramps and bodayache while in the sauna last evening in his cruise accommodation. He underwent a medical examination and precautionary blood tests, which were normal.Despite rest, the following morning, he felt not fully fit to participate in a combat sport. After consultation with his coach, he withdrew on medical grounds," the Indian Olympic Association said in a statement.A bronze medallist at the Asian championships in China in January 2026, Sanyal had entered as a serious medal prospect in MMA, a discipline that is making its debut at the Asian Games.Varun is a first-class business management honours graduate from Queen's Mary University of London. His initial interest in combat sports was influenced by WWE (World Wrestling Entertainment) and TNA (Total Nonstop Action wrestling). A Rocky Balboa fan, Varun’s interest deepened after watching Indian wrestlers Sushil Kumar and Yogeshwar Dutt succeed at the 2012 London Olympics.“Seeing our Olympians succeed really drew me towards martial arts and eventually towards MMA. MMA is, in many ways, the most primal form of sport and competition, so I was naturally drawn to it. It’s also a life skill. Learning how to defend yourself, stay calm under pressure and make decisions when you’re under physical threat are incredibly important skills. Having to make decisions under pressure, sometimes with very serious consequences, has been one of the biggest learnings I’ve taken from MMA,” Varun told SAI Media.Varun comes from a distinguished family with a strong intellectual and public-service background. He is the son of Sanjeev Sanyal, noted economist, author and member of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister of India, and Smita Barooah. His family also has a significant legacy associated with India’s freedom movement, with his great-granduncle Sachindranath Sanyal being a prominent revolutionary and co-founder of the Hindustan Republican Association.Growing up in Singapore, he participated in cricket, football, athletics, squash and powerlifting before progressing to wrestling, Jiu-Jitsu and Muay Thai, and ultimately MMA.“Growing up, I remember my father taking me out to the field and kicking a football around with me. He would take me to play squash, we'd sometimes go on random runs, and he'd make us do exercises together. Even when I was very young, he put me into taekwondo classes, although I wasn't particularly interested in it at the time. As I grew up, whether it was playing cricket, going to the gym, or getting into powerlifting, he was always very supportive.“MMA took him a little bit of time to come around to, but I can't deny how supportive he's been throughout my journey. When it comes to MMA, he's always discussing it with me and trying to understand the sport a little more. He's supportive in whatever way he can be,” said Varun.Asian Games, feels Varun, will be a gamechanger for the sport in India. “The pathway has been a little bumpy. I won the MMA SFI Nationals in 2025, which qualified me for the Asian AMMA Championships in January 2026 in China, where I won a bronze medal. That meant I was officially ranked within the Asian system.“At the time, though, it wasn't particularly clear who had qualified for the Asian Games or what the qualification process was going to look like. There wasn't much clarity from the Asian side about how the qualification process would work. So rather than sitting around waiting, I decided to focus on my professional career.“Eventually, I received final confirmation that I would be going to the Asian Games just two weeks before the Games themselves. So, obviously, preparing mentally and physically for something of this magnitude in such a short period has been quite a challenge. But I suppose that's part of sport. That's what sport is,” said Varun.
Article Summary: Varun Sanyal ruled out of the Asian Games after being declared medically unfit for the competition at the weigh-in process. The athlete felt dizzy at a sauna for weight cut and passed out at the facility. The other MMA fighter in the squad -- Suchika Tariyal -- won her quarter-final bout and confirmed a medal for India.

Article Title: Shafali Verma’s century and India’s bowling blitz crush Bangladesh as defending champions storm into Asian Games final
Article Text:
India into finals (Image: BCCI/X)

Shafali’s historic century powers India to 195

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India bowlers crush Bangladesh’s chase

India set up gold-medal clash against Sri Lanka

Defending champions India Women stormed into the gold-medal match of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 with a commanding 114-run victory over Bangladesh in the semi-final at Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin, Japan.After posting a formidable 195/4 in 20 overs, India’s bowlers dismantled Bangladesh’s chase, bowling them out for just 81 in 15.4 overs. The emphatic win guarantees India a medal and sets up a gold-medal clash against Sri Lanka on September 22.India captain Harmanpreet Kaur won the toss and elected to bat, and the top order made the most of the decision. Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma provided a blistering start, racing to 71 in the powerplay. Mandhana struck 37 off 18 balls before falling, but not before becoming the leading run-scorer in women’s T20I cricket and the first Indian woman to reach 100 sixes in the format.Shafali then took charge, producing a sensational 100 off 49 deliveries, including nine sixes and three fours. She became the first player to score a century in women’s cricket at the Asian Games. Harmanpreet added a valuable 40 off 33 balls as India finished on 195/4, setting Bangladesh a target of 196.Bangladesh’s reply quickly unravelled as they slipped to 9/2 early in the innings. India’s bowlers maintained the pressure, taking wickets at regular intervals and leaving the visitors unable to build a partnership.Dilara Akter offered some resistance with 27 off 23 balls, but the rest of the batting line-up struggled, with eight batters dismissed for single-digit scores.Nandani Sharma and Deepti Sharma led India’s attack with three wickets each. Nandani finished with 3/25, while Deepti returned an economical 3/7. Shree Charani also made an impact with 2/7 as Bangladesh were dismissed for 81 in 15.4 overs.The victory sends India into the gold-medal match, where they will face Sri Lanka on Tuesday, September 22. Sri Lanka booked their place in the final after defeating Pakistan by eight wickets in the first semi-final.India will now look to defend the gold medal they won at the 2022 Asian Games, while Pakistan and Bangladesh will meet in the bronze-medal playoff.
Article Summary: India Women beat Bangladesh by 114 runs in Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 semi- final. Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma hit centuries as India posted 195/4 in 20 overs. Bangladesh were bowled out for just 81 in 15.4 overs. India will now face Sri Lanka in the gold-medal match on September 22.

Article Title: Dilpreet Singh's four-goal show headlines India's 13-1 rout of Indonesia at Asian Games
Article Text:
Asian Games 2026: Dilpreet shines as Indian men's hockey team thrashes Indonesia 13-1

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India's men's hockey team made a commanding start to their Asian Games title defence, cruising past Indonesia 13-1 in their opening Pool A encounter on Sunday.Dilpreet Singh was the standout performer, finding the net four times as the defending champions produced a dominant display. Shilanand Lakra and Sukhjeet Singh chipped in with two goals apiece, while Abhishek, Rajinder Singh, Mandeep Singh Harmanpreet Singh and Jugraj Singh were also on target.Indonesia managed a consolation goal through Aulia Al Ardh in the 33rd minute, but India remained firmly in control for most of the contest.The defending champions needed only six minutes to open the scoring. Harmanpreet's drag flick was kept out by Indonesian goalkeeper Alam Fajar, but Lakra reacted quickest to score from the rebound.Abhishek then doubled India's advantage in the 12th minute, again finishing off a rebound after Fajar had saved the initial effort.Dilpreet took over from there. He made it 3-0 in the 18th minute after converting an assist from Abhishek before finding the net again just a minute later, guiding Sukhjeet's pass home from the far post.India's relentless attacking pressure continued as Rajinder Singh scored from another rebound following a fine attacking move involving Sukhjeet. Mandeep Singh then added another field goal two minutes later to put India 6-0 ahead.The Indians had an opportunity to extend their lead further in the 27th minute when Manpreet Singh was fouled inside the 'D' while attempting to convert a rebound. Harmanpreet stepped up for the resulting penalty stroke, but Fajar made a save with his outstretched right leg.Harmanpreet, however, did not have to wait long for his goal. He converted a penalty corner in the following minute to give India a 7-0 advantage at half-time.Indonesia finally found a breakthrough three minutes into the second half. Al Ardh converted a penalty corner in the 33rd minute to give his side a consolation goal.India quickly resumed their assault. Lakra scored his second of the match in the 35th minute after receiving a well-weighted pass from Rajinder.Dilpreet completed his hat-trick two minutes later, pouncing on a rebound after Fajar had blocked the initial attempt.Sukhjeet then joined the scoring spree in the 38th minute, finding the net with a field goal to make it 10-1.Jugraj Singh converted India's next penalty corner in the 47th minute before Sukhjeet struck again a minute later to complete his brace.Dilpreet saved his best for last, adding his fourth goal in the 49th minute to complete India's 13-1 victory.India will next face Sri Lanka on Tuesday.The match also marked the first Asian Games appearance of India's new primary saffron kits. Despite Hockey India president Dilip Tirkey's earlier claim that both Indian teams would wear their traditional blue jerseys at the Games, the men's and women's sides have instead turned out in the saffron kits first worn during the recent World Cup in the Netherlands and Belgium.
Article Summary: India's men's hockey team made a commanding start to their Asian Games title defence, cruising past Indonesia 13-1 in their opening Pool A encounter on Sunday. Dilpreet Singh was the standout performer, finding the net four times as the defending champions produced a dominant display. Shilanand Lakra and Sukhjeet Singh chipped in with two goals apiece, while Abhishek, Rajinder Singh, Mandeep Singh Harmanpreet and Jugraj Singh were also on target.

The Asian Games 2026 got underway in Aichi-Nagoya on Sunday with India making a strong start to their medal campaign, picking up two silver medals in the women's 10m air rifle competition. Elavenil Valarivan was at the centre of India's opening-day medal rush, winning individual silver after earlier helping the country secure silver in the team event alongside Sonam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod.In the individual final, Elavenil produced a score of 252.4 points to finish behind Japan's Hinata Taichi, who won gold with an Asian Games record 253.0. South Korea's Hyojin Ban claimed bronze with 230.4.Elavenil entered the final two shots just 0.3 points behind Taichi and remained firmly in contention after shooting 10.4 to the Japanese shooter's 10.6, which stretched the gap to 0.5 points. Article Title: Elavenil Valarivan narrowly misses out on gold, settles for women’s 10m air rifle silver at Asian Games 2026
Article Text:
Elavenil Valarivan (Image credit: X)

From team silver to individual silver

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Elavenil Valarivan narrowly missed out on gold after producing a strong performance in the women’s 10m air rifle individual final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, settling for silver with a cumulative score of 252.4.Japan’s Taichi Hinata clinched gold with 253.0, while South Korea’s Ban Hyojin took bronze with 230.4.The 27-year-old Indian shooter was in contention for the top spot throughout the final but fell just 0.6 points short of Hinata. The silver adds to the medal she had already won in the team event and further underlines her consistency at the Games.Elavenil had earlier combined with Sonam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod to win silver in the women’s 10m air rifle team event, giving India its first medal of the Aichi-Nagoya Games.The Indian trio finished with a team total of 1898 points, behind gold medallists China, while Japan finished fourth.Elavenil was India's standout performer in the team competition, scoring 633.5 points to qualify for the individual final. Sonam also made the final and finished sixth with a cumulative score of 167.0.The individual final featured a strong Asian field, with shooters from India, Japan, China and South Korea.Elavenil was drawn at firing point E in the start list, alongside compatriot Sonam, Japan’s Taichi Hinata and Nobata Misaki, China’s Han Jiayu and Wang Zifei, and South Korea’s Ban Hyojin and Kwon Yuna.Having already contributed to India’s team silver, Elavenil entered the individual competition with another medal opportunity and remained firmly in the gold-medal race until the closing stages.Her silver gives India a second medal in the women’s 10m air rifle competition and keeps the shooting contingent at the centre of the country’s medal campaign.Earlier, Suchika Tariyal also assured India of a medal after defeating Mongolia’s Altanchimeg Baigalmaa to reach the semifinals of the women’s traditional 60kg MMA event. Her win secured India’s first-ever Asian Games medal in MMA, which is making its debut at the Games.For Elavenil, however, the event ended with silver, a strong finish, but one that came agonisingly close to gold.
Article Summary: Elavenil Valarivan wins silver in the women's 10m air rifle individual final. The 27-year-old Indian shooter was in contention for the top spot throughout the final but fell just 0.6 points short of Taichi Hinata. Elavenil had earlier combined with Sonam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod to win team silver. Suchika Tariyal secured India’s first-ever Asian Games medal in MMA.

Article Title: Champions return, 314 debutants arrive: Inside India’s 500-plus Asian Games campaign
Article Text:
India eye record medals at Asian Games 2026

Mirabai Chanu ’s missing Asian Games medal

NEW DELHI: Hoping to build on the historic campaign three years back at Hangzhou, India begins its campaign at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya with a 500-plus athlete contingent, aiming to better the 106-medal tally racked up at the last Games.While the build-up to the Games has been marred by mismanagement, an accommodation crisis and the threat of a typhoon looming large over the Japanese prefecture, for the athletes, once the Games begin, it will be, as the adage goes, ‘game mode on’.The 500-plus athlete Indian contingent comprises a sizeable group of returning champions and experienced campaigners. 314 of those athletes are preparing for their first appearance at the continental event.Interestingly, women athletes make up 46.7% of the contingent. At 15, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is the youngest member. Equestrian rider Shruti Vora, 55, is the oldest.India will compete in 256 events across 36 of the 43 sports at Aichi-Nagoya, with the Games beginning on September 19 and running until October 4.Avinash Sable, returning from a year-long injury, will try to defend his men's 3000m steeplechase title, while Tajinderpal Singh Toor returns in the men's shot put.Parul Chaudhary will be another athlete trying to defend her women's 5000m crown, while India's men's 4x400m relay team will also go into the Games as defending champions.In badminton, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty will aim to defend their men's doubles title. Their gold in Hangzhou was India's first Asian Games title in the event.Indian compound archers swept all five gold medals in the discipline at Hangzhou, and returning champion Jyothi Surekha Vennam will be the fulcrum around whom India's archery campaign will revolve.Then there are athletes whose Asian Games story is still waiting for a first chapter.Mirabai Chanu has won a world title, Olympic silver and Commonwealth Games gold. The Asian Games medal remains missing from her collection.The 32-year-old will lead India's four-member weightlifting team in Aichi-Nagoya, with Gyaneshwari Yadav, Seram Nirupama Devi and Harjinder Kaur completing the squad.Chanu missed the 2018 Asian Games because of injury and did not compete at Hangzhou. Now, after a career that has already included a world championship title, an Olympic medal and multiple Commonwealth Games titles, the Asian Games is the major multi-sport medal still absent from her cabinet.Anahat Singh is another young Indian athlete arriving in Japan with a title already behind her.The 18-year-old is a World Junior Squash Champion and has made the transition from junior squash to the senior international circuit at a young age.She is part of India's eight-member squash team in Aichi-Nagoya. Joshana Chinappa, Tanvi Khanna and Shameena Riaz are the other members of the women's squad, while Abhay Singh, Velavan Senthilkumar, Veer Chotrani and Suraj Kumar Chand make up the men's team.Squash was among India's gold-medal sports at Hangzhou.Shooting will once again be one of the major sports to follow, with 27 events on India's programme.The contingent had bagged 22 medals at Hangzhou, including seven golds.Manu Bhaker returns in the women's squad alongside the in-form Esha Singh, Rahi Sarnobat, Elavenil Valarivan, Ashi Chouksey, Suruchi Singh and Tilottama Sen.The men's group includes Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar, Rudrankksh Patil and Anish Bhanwala.There will also be a sizable shotgun shooters' bunch, with the veteran Mairaj Ahmed Khan leading the pack alongside Kynan Chenai, Shapath Bharadwaj and Ahvar Rizvi. Neeru Dhanda, Manisha Keer, Maheshwari Chauhan and Parinaaz Dhaliwal are also part of the shotgun group.Neeraj Chopra, meanwhile, will not be in Japan. The javelin thrower, who defended his Asian Games title in Hangzhou, is missing the 2026 Games after an ankle ligament injury during training.Athletics has the largest athlete representation, with 78 competitors, and also has the biggest programme with 43 events. They had bagged a total of 29 medals, including six golds, at Hangzhou, and the expectation will be to go many a medal better this time around.Alongside Sable, Toor and Parul are names such as Gulveer Singh, Animesh Kujur, Harita Bhadra, Jyothi Yarraji, Murali Sreeshankar, Praveen Chithravel and Tejaswin Shankar.The men's hockey team goes into Aichi-Nagoya as the defending Asian Games champion, but its recent World Cup campaign has left a different question hanging over the side.India won gold in Hangzhou in 2023, beating Japan 5-1 in the final, and the title also secured direct qualification for the Paris Olympics. The team now has another Olympic berth at stake in Japan, with the Asian Games gold medallist earning direct qualification for Los Angeles 2028.The women's team comes to Japan with a more encouraging recent result.India finished fifth at the 2026 Women's Hockey World Cup, their best finish at the tournament in 52 years. The campaign included a 2-2 draw against China, the 2024 Olympic silver medallists, a result that carried particular weight after India's 4-0 defeat to the same opposition in the Hangzhou Asian Games semifinal.The women's team has not won the Asian Games since 1982, and gold in Aichi-Nagoya would also bring direct qualification for the 2028 Olympics. Salima Tete will captain the side, with Savita Punia, Lalremsiami, Navneet Kaur, Deepika and Nikki Pradhan among the experienced players in the squad.India's men's T20 team is led by Shreyas Iyer and includes Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson, Ishan Kishan, Shivam Dube, Tilak Varma, Axar Patel, Washington Sundar, Jasprit Bumrah and Arshdeep Singh.Sooryavanshi is also part of the squad.Harmanpreet Kaur leads the women's side, with Smriti Mandhana, Shafali Verma, Deepti Sharma, Richa Ghosh and Renuka Thakur among the selected players.India won both the men's and women's T20 gold medals at Hangzhou.There will also be Indian participation in four esports events - eFootball, Puyo Puyo Champions, League of Legends and Pokemon Unite.Haryana leads the state-wise numbersHaryana has the largest representation with 96 athletes.Maharashtra follows with 49, Tamil Nadu 37, Punjab 35, Manipur 34, Uttar Pradesh 32 and Delhi 30.Karnataka, Kerala and Madhya Pradesh have 24 athletes each.The representation stretches across the country, with athletes also coming from Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Mizoram, Nagaland, Puducherry, Tripura, Sikkim, Ladakh and Lakshadweep.The support structure behind the contingent is spread across several programmes. National Coaching Camps account for 134 athletes, followed by TOPS Development with 78 and TOPS Core with 77. Khelo India has 65 athletes, TAGG 48 and National Centres of Excellence 25.Aichi-Nagoya therefore brings together a group that already knows the Asian Games podium and another that has never experienced it.Mirabai Chanu still has one major medal to add. Anahat Singh arrives as a world junior champion. Manu Bhaker and Aishwary Pratap lead another large shooting group, while Sable, Toor, Parul, Jyothi and Satwik-Chirag return as defending champions.And around them are 314 first-timers, spread across 256 events in 36 sports.
Article Summary: India will compete in 256 events across 36 of the 43 sports at Aichi-Nagoya, with the Games beginning on September 19 and running until October 4. The 500-plus athlete Indian contingent comprises a sizeable group of returning champions and experienced campaigners. At 15, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is the youngest member of the Indian contingent.

Article Title: Japan’s Takumi Hojo scripts history in front of home crowd, wins first gold of Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
Article Text:
Gold medallist Japan's Takumi Hojo celebrates on the podium (Image: Reuters)

Hojo pulls away in the final run

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Japan’s first gold gives team a boost

Japan got the perfect start to its home Asian Games campaign as Takumi Hojo stormed to victory in the men’s individual triathlon on Sunday, claiming the first gold medal of the Aichi-Nagoya Games.The 30-year-old produced a decisive final run to finish in 52 minutes and 56 seconds, edging China’s Zhang Xirui by nine seconds. Kazakhstan’s Arlan Zhanabay secured bronze, crossing the finish line 15 seconds behind Hojo.The victory marked a memorable moment for the host nation, with Hojo adding an individual gold to the mixed relay title he won at the Hangzhou Asian Games three years ago.The men’s individual triathlon featured a 750-metre swim, a 20-kilometre cycling leg and a 5km run. Hojo was fourth out of the water in Mikawa Bay before moving into fifth position during the cycling section. He then made his move on the final run, battling closely with Zhang before pulling clear in the closing stretch.“I was really fired-up. Even the rain held off and I was in top form right up until I stood on the starting line," added Hojo, who also won the Asian Games test triathlon a year ago on the same course.“(I knew) it would be tough, but (I thought) I would push myself and if it works, I think it will be a good race," said the 30-year-old Hojo, whose victory will qualify him for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.Hojo said winning the opening gold had lifted the Japanese contingent and provided momentum for the rest of the competition.“As it’s our first gold medal, it’s given the Japanese team a real boost,” he said, adding that he hoped to pass that momentum on to the women’s team and his teammates in the relay.Zhang finished second in 53:05, while Zhanabay took bronze in 53:11. Uzbekistan’s Aleksandr Kurishov, who was first out of the water, faded during the cycling and eventually finished 20th. Swimming competitions also began on Sunday at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre as the Asian Games moved into action across multiple sports.
Article Summary: Takumi Hojo wins first gold of the Aichi-Nagoya Games. 30-year-old finishes ahead of China's Zhang Xirui by nine seconds. Kazakhstan's Arlan Zhanabay claims bronze medal. Hojo will qualify for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

NEW DELHI: The 46th edition of the Chess Olympiad began on a murky note, with multiple teams facing accommodation issues upon arrival in host city Samarkand, Uzbekistan. India, the defending champions across both the open and women's sections, also had to wait for hours before players were allotted separate rooms. Coming off a gruelling week back home for the Global Chess League (GCL), one of the players who had to hop straight from the Bengaluru event to Samarkand was India's No. 2 Arjun Erigaisi.When Praggnanandhaa opted to rest for the opening-day fixture against Thailand, it was Arjun who stepped in to play Board 1. Playing white, he lost to Thailand's 2363-rated International Master Prin Laohawirapap.World champion Gukesh, who has had a commendable score of 3.5/4 in this tournament, explained what had gone wrong for Arjun. "Arjun's first game was very unfortunate, but also worth mentioning that we had very hectic travel and then the first day there were some organisation issues," Gukesh said in an interview with FIDE after his Round 3 win over Italy's Sabino Brunello. "So, Arjun got a room probably a few hours before he went. I mean, we all waited for like six hours to get a room. So obviously, in the first round, Arjun was just tired, and he blundered in the end."Gukesh added that things had improved since then. "The first day was a bit tricky for all of us, but after that, I think we are all rested. We are all looking forward to the games and all good," he said.Those words showed up in the results on Saturday, when Arjun took down Maksim Chigaev to secure his first win of the tournament, helping India beat Spain 3-1.Arjun Erigaisi, playing white, produced a controlled attacking performance against Maksim Chigaev.The opening was a flexible Réti/English setup, with White gaining space through 12.h4 and 13.h5, provoking ...g5 and creating long-term kingside targets.After 14.d5, White secured a useful space advantage while Black’s pieces became somewhat passive.The key strategic phase began with 17.Nh2 and 18.Bh3, followed by the exchange of bishops on c8. Erigaisi then expanded with 21.e4 and 23.f4, correctly opening lines while Black’s king remained vulnerable.The sequence 28.Qe4 Rxf1 29.Rxf1 Rf8 30.Rxf8+ simplified the rooks and left White with a dangerous queen-and-knight attack.The decisive phase was 31.Qh7, followed by 32.Qh8+ and 33.Ng4, coordinating queen and knight around the exposed king. After 34.Nxe5+, Black could not escape the perpetual-looking checks, and 36.Qf7+ ended the game.Elsewhere on the board, Gukesh continued his fine run, beating Spain's Alexei Shirov to move to 4.5/5 and continuing a solid turnaround from Thursday's dip below the 2700 rating mark.Praggnanandhaa and Nihal Sarin both drew their games, enough for India to close out the tie 3-1.For Erigaisi specifically, the win carries added significance. As India's second-highest rated player and a regular on Board 1 or 2 duty, a winless start would have added pressure to an already long season that had him travelling directly from the GCL in Bengaluru to Samarkand with barely any time to recover. Saturday's result suggests that adjustment period may now be behind him.India's women's team also kept their unbeaten run alive, beating Mongolia 3-1. Koneru Humpy and Vaishali Rameshbabu both drew their games against lower-rated opposition.But Divya Deshmukh and Savitha Shri won on the lower boards to see the team through comfortably, continuing a campaign that has yet to drop a match tie.With both squads now through four rounds without a defeat as a team, the tests only get tougher from here. India will take on Poland in the women's section on Sunday, while the open team faces a mouthwatering clash against Anish Giri's Dutch side, arguably the sternest test either Indian team has faced so far in Samarkand.
Article Summary: Arjun Erigaisi, playing white, produced a controlled attacking performance against Maksim Chigaev. Gukesh Praggnanandhaa and Nihal Sarin both drew their games for India to close out the tie 3-1. India's women's team also kept their unbeaten run alive, beating Mongolia 3-0.

When South Zone and East Zone faced-off in the Duleep Trophy final, captain Tilak Varma’s team was widely considered as the favourite. South Zone were not only playing at home, but had added in-form batter Devdutt Paddikal and Test regular Mohammed Siraj to the playing XI. There was a difference in pedigree too. South Zone were 19-time winners and East Zone had taken home the inter-zonal trophy only twice, the last in 2012-13.But matches are not decided by reputation or history. East outplayed the hosts in every area, including hunger and self-belief to win the trophy. Even the sparse Chennai crowd clapped for the visiting side, especially for captain Ishan Kishan, a reborn cricketer whose monumental 270 first set an uphill task for Varma’s side, and whose feisty 80 shut the door on South’s faint revival hopes in the second.In the 1980s and earlier, East Zone were mostly also-rans in Duleep Trophy. The inter-zonal trophy began in 1961-62, but EZ won its first title only in 2011-12, with Wriddhiman Saha and Shami being the key to that triumph. Next season, Jharkhand’s underappreciated Ishank Jaggi’s ton fashioned East’s repeat success.Now, Jharkhand is a potent force in domestic cricket. In Dec 2025, the mineral-rich state claimed the T20 Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy for the first time. Is it any surprise that Kishan scored a ton in the final and was Player of the Match, as in the Duleep Trophy final?Carved out of Bihar, Jharkhand became a separate state in 2000 — a reason why its biggest star, MS Dhoni, began his first-class career playing for (then) Rabri Devi ruled state in 1999.Kishan comes from Bihar, whose cricket association was mired in controversy for years. But several other Jharkhand players, who excelled with the bat in the Duleep final, are born and bred in the fledgling picturesque state. Kumar Kushagra, the 21-year-old ’keeper who stroked to 101 and 46 in the final and is part of the India ‘A’ squad, was born in the steel city of Bokaro. The Dhanbad-born 23-year-old offie Mohammed Kounain Quraishi cruised to 116 in the second innings while claiming the vital wicket of Varma. But Ranchi-born Shikhar Mohan was the stand-out newbie. The 21-year-old southpaw contributed with 85 and 52, displaying calm under pressure in the second innings. He was not only a livewire in the outfield but also stepped in as a left-arm spinner and claimed two wickets when senior Anukul Roy, another Jharkhand-born player, hurt his bowling finger.This was a team triumph. On pitches with different requirements, Bengal pacers Mukesh Kumar and Shami were better than their opposite numbers in both the semis and final. The tournament was a test for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s red-ball credentials. He demonstrated that he can adjust, even dominate. He remains a work in progress, especially against spin. The teenager must be evaluated not only by the runs he scores, but the way he scores them.Irrespective of where they ply their trade, players born in Bihar and Jharkhand are the fulcrum of the new rising East. There was a time when the zonal side was dominated by home-grown Bengal players. Barring Sudeep Gharami, every other player representing Bengal in the final’s playing XI was a cricket migrant.
Article Summary: South Zone were 19-time winners and East Zone had taken home the inter-zonal trophy only twice, the last in 2012-13. East outplayed the hosts in every area, including hunger and self-belief to win the trophy. Even the sparse Chennai crowd clapped for the visiting side.

Article Title: Denied by visa row in 2023, former Asia No. 1 Rupa Bayor finally gets her Games shot

KOLKATA: When Rupa Bayor qualified for the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023, the taekwondo poomsae specialist from Arunachal Pradesh believed she had a genuine shot at finishing on the podium.Instead, she watched from afar after being denied the opportunity to compete because of the visa issue involving athletes from Arunachal Pradesh.“It was very painful at the time because I felt I had a genuine chance of winning a medal,” Rupa told TOI in an exclusive interaction. “But some things are beyond your control. Eventually, you have to move forward and focus on the future.”Three years later, the 26-year-old gets her long-awaited Asiad debut as one of India’s medal hopes in taekwondo poomsae after a remarkable rise that saw her become the first Indian poomsae athlete to reach Asia No. 1 and a career-high world No. 5 earlier this year, although she is currently ranked second in Asia and seventh in the world.Her coach, Abhishek Dubey, believes the disappointment of missing the previous Games ultimately made her stronger.“At that time, she was already among the top-ranked athletes in Asia and we felt she had a genuine chance of winning a medal,” said Dubey, who has been involved in the sport for around 36 years as a coach, administrator and sports management professional.“An athlete’s career is short and the Asian Games come only once every four years. It was extremely disappointing, but we decided to stay focused and continue training. Fortunately, we managed to do that and now we are in a position where we genuinely believe a medal is possible.”The journey to this point, however, has been anything but conventional.Raised in the Daporijo area of Arunachal’s Upper Subansiri district, Rupa was introduced to combat sports by her maternal uncle, Tabu Sera, who practised karate. Back then, international competitions felt impossibly distant.“At the grassroots level, the Asian Games felt like a distant dream,” she recalled. “We didn’t have international athletes around us, so our mindset was simply to participate in competitions and come back home.”Behind Rupa’s rise also lies a story of resilience. She lost her father at a very young age and was raised by her mother, a farmer who supported the family in rural Arunachal. Growing up far from India’s sporting centres, the odds of reaching an event like the Asian Games seemed remote.But everything changed in 2021 when she moved to Navi Mumbai to train under Dubey.“I was looking for a good place to train for a long time,” she said. “When I saw the athletes he was coaching and the results they were achieving, I felt he was the right coach for me.”Dubey still remembers the day she arrived in Mumbai. “She just landed up with her bags and wanted to train,” he said. “What stood out immediately was her competitiveness and willingness to learn.”That discipline has translated into results. Rupa has won medals consistently on the international circuit and defeated several best athletes of Asia, including competitors who medalled at the previous Asian Games.This year, she won bronze at the Asian Taekwondo Poomsae Championships in Ulaanbaatar, becoming the first Indian athlete to win medals in two consecutive editions of the continental event.The dream that once seemed out of reach is thus now within touching distance. And after spending three years waiting for a chance that was taken away from her, Rupa, currently in South Korea for the 2026 World Taekwondo Poomsae Championships, has only one goal in mind.“My mindset is no longer about just participating,” she said. “Whenever I compete, I want to win a medal.”
Article Summary: Rupa Bayor is the first Indian poomsae athlete to reach Asia No. 1 and a career- high world No. 5. The 26-year-old is currently ranked second in Asia and seventh in the world. Rupa won bronze at the Asian Taekwondo Poomsae Championships in Ulaanbaatar this year.

NEW DELHI: When Isharani Baruah looks at India’s badminton squad for the Asian Games , she doesn’t see a team overawed by Asia’s traditional powerhouses.The 22-year-old from Assam will make her Asian Games debut in Aichi-Nagoya, stepping into a squad that brings together the experience of two-time Olympic medallist PV Sindhu and the emergence of youngsters such as Tanvi Sharma, Unnati Hooda and the doubles pair of Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand.For Isharani, the journey to this stage began almost by accident. Growing up in Dibrugarh, she was a regular fixture among the boys playing different kinds of sport in her neighbourhood. A neighbour noticed her enthusiasm and suggested badminton to her mother. There was no sporting pedigree at home, no elaborate plan for a career in badminton — just a young girl, a racquet and an opportunity that changed the course of her life.India’s medal ambitions in Aichi-Nagoya come against a backdrop of steady progress on the Asian circuit. The gap with China, Japan and other established powers may still exist, but Indian players are increasingly finding themselves on the latter stages of tournaments rather than merely entering them.For Isharani, the evidence is there week after week.“If you see the Super 100 and Super 300 tournaments, there are always three or four Indians reaching the quarterfinals or semifinals.Even in the 500s, we’re competing well. Badminton has definitely grown in India, and we’re going to reach the level of countries like China and Japan quite soon. We’re ready to challenge these powerhouses at the Asian Games,” she said.Her own rise has followed that same route. Consistent performances on the lower-tier circuit have helped her climb the rankings and, more importantly, exposed her to opponents from the badminton-heavy nations of Asia.“To reach the Super 750 and 1000 events, you first have to perform in the 100s and 300s because that’s how you earn ranking points. Playing against Chinese and Japanese opponents there and beating them gives us confidence before the bigger tournaments,” Isharani said.But perhaps the biggest change in her game has not been technical. It has been between the ears. Once prone to tightening up after mistakes, Isharani has learned to treat composure as part of her game plan. The smile that often appears on court is not simply an expression of enjoyment; it has become a way of resetting herself.“For me, the most important thing is to enjoy playing. Even if I’m making mistakes, I don’t want to become tense because then I lose focus on the next point. I keep smiling, I talk to my coaches more, and I trust the process,” she said.
Article Summary: Isharani Baruah will make her Asian Games debut in Aichi-Nagoya. The 22-year-old is part of India's badminton squad for the Asian Games. India’s medal ambitions come against a backdrop of steady progress on the Asian circuit.

Article Title: 'I'm hoping for gold': Star golfer Khalin Joshi backs India’s Asian Games golf teams for medal success
Article Text:
Khalin Joshi. (File Pic - TOI Photo)

NEW DELHI: With the Asian Games beginning in Japan's Aichi-Nagoya, golfer Khalin Joshi has backed India's men's and women's golf teams to challenge for medals.The men's squad features in-form professionals who have excelled both domestically and on the DP World Tour, while the women's team boasts experienced international campaigners.“We have a great team. Yuvraj has been playing excellent golf in Europe, Saptak is leading the Order of Merit, and all of them are riding high on confidence,” he said.“I'm really hopeful they're going to contend. I'm hoping for gold, and I just hope both the men's and women's teams keep the Indian flag flying high.”Joshi insists there has been no dramatic swing change, no new coach and no technical overhaul behind one of the ost consistent spells of his season. The Bengaluru golfer believes the biggest transformation has happened where scores are often decided in the mind.Fresh off his victory at the Nava Raipur Open on Friday, Joshi said “I haven't changed anything much, to be honest. I've just tried to work on my mental game and stay more in the present throughout the round.”That approach proved crucial in Raipur, where relentless rain forced officials to shorten the event to 36 holes.With only nine holes played on each of the final two days, golfers had little room for recovery, making fast starts essential.Rather than playing conservatively, Joshi embraced the conditions. “The moment we heard it was reduced to 36 holes, we knew we had to start from the get-go. Everyone had limited holes, so my mindset was to be aggressive,” he said.“The course was soft, which actually favoured attacking golf. You could hit your numbers and be more aggressive towards the flags.”The win comes at a time when Indian professional golf is enjoying unprecedented depth. Nearly every PGTI event this season has produced tightly contested leaderboards, with established names and emerging youngsters regularly challenging for titles.Joshi believes the increasing prize money and professionalism of the domestic circuit have fundamentally changed the competitive landscape. “The PGTI is very competitive now. We're very top-heavy and the top 20 to 25 players can win on any given week,” he said.He pointed to the current form of golfers including Saptak Talwar, Rashid Khan, Honey Baisoya, Akshay Sharma, Om Prakash Chouhan, Viraj Madappa, Kartik Singh, Kritish Batra and Shubham Jaglan as evidence of the circuit's strength. “People are working harder in the gym and on the golf course. Golf in India is growing by leaps and bounds, and it's only a matter of time before we see many more Indians succeeding internationally. ”While technical preparation remains important, Joshi's tournament routine is deliberately uncomplicated. The 33-year-old avoids adding pressure before decisive rounds and instead focuses on slowing everything down. “I sleep well before tournaments and try not to rush anything in the morning,” he said. “I give myself ample time for breakfast, warming up and getting to the tee. Whenever I hurry, things start going haywire. The key for me is to stay slow and just breeze into the first tee.”Interestingly, Joshi says he learns as much from conversations with contemporaries as from senior professionals. Among those he frequently discusses golf with is close friend and DP World Tour regular Shubhankar Sharma. “Shubhankar is a really good friend. We talk regularly about our games and what we're feeling,” Joshi revealed. “Honestly, I try to learn from everybody.It can be a senior player or even a youngster everyone has something valuable to offer. ”That openness extends to the increasingly close-knit atmosphere on the Indian tour, where fierce competition coexists with genuine camaraderie.Joshi believes that culture, combined with rising financial opportunities, is inspiring more young golfers to treat the sport as a viable profession.The Raipur champion has little time to celebrate. He returns to action this week at his home course, the Karnataka Golf Association, before a week's break ahead of the Tour Championship at Jaypee Greens and the lucrative DP World India Championship from Oct 15-18 at the Delhi Golf Club where only the top 24 players on the Order of Merit will tee up.For a golfer whose biggest victory this season was built on quieting the mind, the objective remains unchanged. “Just stay present everything else takes care of itself.”
Article Summary: Golfer Khalin Joshi has backed India's men's and women's golf teams to challenge for medals at the Asian Games. The 33-year-old is fresh off his victory at the Nava Raipur Open on Friday. He believes the increasing prize money and professionalism of the domestic circuit have fundamentally changed the competitive landscape.

Article Title: Asian Games: Several Indian athletes await ceremonial kits, Tajinderpal Singh Toor episode raises questions
Article Text:
India's Tajinderpal Singh Toor (PTI Photo)

Poll Vote & Share your view Should the Indian Olympic Association improve their kit management and communication processes? Yes, definitely. No, it's not a big issue. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NAGOYA/NEW DELHI: If the first controversy involving the Indian contingent at the Asian Games was expected to take time to surface, it did not. It came less than 24 hours before the opening ceremony.In a last-minute change in Nagoya on Friday night, the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) replaced defending shot put champion Tajinderpal Singh Toor with kabaddi star Pawan Sehrawat as the Indian flagbearer alongside Manu Bhaker for Saturday’s opening ceremony.The dramatic turn of events unfolded after Toor, who had earlier spoken of his pride at being named flagbearer, realised that he did not have the ceremonial kit required for the opening and closing ceremonies.All athletes are provided the ceremonial kit as part of their Games kit, irrespective of whether they attend the opening ceremony. So what went wrong?TOI understands that prior to departure for the Games, Toor had received a ceremonial kit in the wrong size, which was sent back for alteration. The altered kit, however, did not reach him before his departure.Toor trained at the National Institute of Sports in Patiala before joining the track and field contingent in New Delhi for the official send-off and Indian Athletics Finals Series on September 10.He then travelled to the University of Tsukuba for the pre-Games training camp.Sources said the issue came to a head on Friday night, with the ceremonial kit still unavailable in Nagoya. Toor was quoted as saying he had informed the IOA that he would be unable to attend the ceremony as the kit was not expected to reach him before 3pm on Saturday — three hours before the ceremony.The IOA initially attributed the replacement to “technical” reasons. Toor was also initially said to have forgotten to carry his ceremonial kit, a version that he subsequently disputed.“Looks like he has been told to say that he forgot to carry his kit in India when he had received none,” a source alleged.It has since emerged that the issue was more complicated, with several athletes yet to receive their ceremonial kits.“There was miscommunication between the athlete, AFI and IOA on the issue. If the athlete is carrying with him his playing and training kits from India, he should also pack the ceremonial kit,” a source said.Sources said the IOA contingent staff in Aichi-Nagoya should have checked with the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) whether its athletes had received their ceremonial kits before announcing Toor’s name. Likewise, the AFI should have confirmed with the athlete before forwarding his name.The issue was compounded by the fact that more than 100 Indian athletes were reportedly yet to receive their ceremonial kits. With the contingent expanding and last-minute requirements having to be met from the available stock, officials were racing against time.Toor, who is set to defend his shot put title, eventually took responsibility publicly for the episode. But the last-minute replacement exposed a communication gap between the athlete, federation and IOA — and raised questions over the coordination.
Article Summary: Defending shot put champion Tajinderpal Singh Toor replaced with kabaddi star Pawan Sehrawat as the Indian flagbearer for Saturday’s opening ceremony. The dramatic turn of events unfolded after Toor realised that he did not have the ceremonial kit required for the opening and closing ceremonies.

Article Title: 'Vaibhav Sooryavanshi can't transition to Test cricket': Ex-cricketer says 'he doesn't have the technique'
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (PTI Photo)

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi may still be only 15, but the sheer impact of his performances has already led to questions about whether he can eventually conquer all three formats. The Samastipur-born left-hander has made a stunning start to his career, with his exploits in the IPL and at the international level putting him firmly under the spotlight.His immediate future, however, remains in T20 cricket. Sooryavanshi did not feature in any of the matches, with Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma preferred at the top of the order. Given the team's desire to maintain continuity, the decision was understandable despite the teenager's impressive IPL campaign.The discussion has now moved beyond the teenager's place in India's T20I XI, with his potential in Test cricket becoming another talking point. Sooryavanshi has limited red-ball experience and is nowhere close to a Test call-up at present, but former England spinner Monty Panesar has already offered his assessment of whether the youngster can make the transition to the longest format.Speaking on the Beyond23 Cricket Podcast alongside former Australia captain Michael Clarke , Panesar questioned whether Sooryavanshi possesses the technique required to succeed in Test cricket.“I can’t see Sooryavanshi transitioning to Test cricket. Harry Brook is the only one right now who’s in the top 10 in Tests and T20Is. But I just don’t think Sooryavanshi has got the technique," Panesar said.Clarke, however, offered a contrasting view. The former Australia captain argued that players can succeed across all three formats if they have the necessary skill and talent, pointing to Virat Kohli and AB de Villiers as examples.“I think you can still play all three formats. Virat Kohli and AB de Villiers showed that. These guys were brilliant Test cricketers and unbelievable T20 cricketers as well. If a player from this generation, like Sooryavanshi, can make the transition into Test cricket, it is going to be unreal to watch," said Clarke.Clarke also highlighted Sooryavanshi's power and exceptional ability to read the ball as his biggest strengths at this stage of his career. He believes the technical aspects of the youngster's batting can develop with greater exposure to different conditions.“Right now, power is still his main thing, and he has an amazing eye. He picks the ball as well as any young cricketer in the world. The technique will get better the more he tours with India and trains in different conditions," said Sooryavanshi.Clarke went a step further in backing the teenager's long-term potential, suggesting he has the talent to become a star across formats if he chooses to pursue that route."He’s talented enough that, if he wants to do it, I can’t see any reason why he can’t be a superstar in all three formats," he added.Sooryavanshi has already had some exposure to red-ball cricket. He was part of the East Zone side that won the Duleep Trophy and came close to scoring a century in the semi-final against Central Zone before being dismissed in the 90s.
Article Summary: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has made a stunning start to his career. The 15-year-old was left out of India's T20I XI against Sri Lanka. Former England spinner Monty Panesar questioned whether he can succeed in Test cricket. But former Australia captain Michael Clarke believes he can be a star in all three formats.

MUMBAI: The BCCI’s position on the National Sports Governance Act dominated discussions at the board’s 95th annual general meeting on Friday, with secretary Devajit Saikia saying the body would comply with the law once cricket is officially notified as a designated sport.Saikia, however, said the BCCI would not come under the RTI Act because it does not receive govt grants. He said the board pays about Rs 3,000 crore annually in income tax, unlike other national sports federations that receive govt funding. “Regarding the Sports Act, our stand is very clear,” Saikia said after the AGM. “There are a lot of things yet to be done by the concerned authority. Once those exercises are completed, and once BCCI comes under the Sports Act, a notification has to be issued to make cricket a designated sport. Till that time, we are not supposed to do anything.”Saikia said the BCCI would respond to the Supreme Court on Oct 27, when the matter is next listed. “Whenever that notification comes, we will immediately act and do our work as per the rules of the new sports act.” Saikia also argued that cricket should not be treated like other govt-funded sports bodies. “We are paying 3,000 crore in tax annually to the govt. Unlike other sports federations, we don’t take any govt funding.Hence, cricket cannot be treated as a designated sport under the National Sports Governance Act 2025,” he said.The BCCI will complete 100 years in Dec 2028 and plans to form a committee for year-long centenary celebrations beginning in Dec 2027. Saikia said the board also discussed plans to mark the 20th edition of the IPL next year.“In Dec 2028, we will complete 100 years of the BCCI, so we will hold centenary celebrations from Dec 2027 for one year,” he said. “The IPL, which will start from March-end next year, will have its 20th edition. We have discussed that it should be done in a grand way.”
Article Summary: The BCCI will comply with the law once cricket is officially notified as a designated sport. Secretary Devajit Saikia said the BCCI would not come under the RTI Act because it does not receive govt grants. He said the board pays about Rs 3,000 crore annually in income tax.

West Indies have brought back experienced opener John Campbell for their upcoming ODI series against India, while Kamil Pooran has received his first T20I call-up. The Caribbean side will face India in three ODIs and five T20Is from September 27 to October 17, with the series spread across eight cities.Campbell returns after missing the last two ODIs against New Zealand because of a hamstring injury. Captain Shai Hope will lead the 15-member ODI squad, which also includes young batter Jewel Andrew. Andrew replaces Ackeem Auguste, who is still recovering from surgery he underwent in August.Shimron Hetmyer, who featured in West Indies' final two ODIs against New Zealand, has been left out of the ODI squad. However, he will return for the T20I series after being given additional time to recover following the Caribbean Premier League.The first two ODIs against India will bring the automatic qualification phase for the 2027 ICC Men's ODI World Cup to an end. West Indies, however, will have to play a qualification tournament early next year after failing to finish ahead of their closest rivals in the standings.Head coach Daren Sammy believes the India series will give his team a valuable chance to test themselves against the world's top-ranked ODI and T20I side and prepare for the World Cup."Playing against the top team in the world presents us with a chance to fine tune and improve our performances as an ODI team which has seen quality performances across the cycle," Sammy said.In the T20I squad, the biggest talking point is the inclusion of Kamil, who has earned his maiden call-up after an impressive recent run. The right-handed opener scored 273 runs in eight innings at a strike rate of 159.64 and an average of 39.Quentin Sampson, who was part of West Indies' T20 World Cup squad earlier this year in India, has also been selected. Experienced all-rounder Jason Holder, meanwhile, has been rested.West Indies ODI squad: Shai Hope (captain), Jewel Andrew, John Campbell, Keacy Carty, Roston Chase, Matthew Forde, Justin Greaves, Amir Jangoo, Alzarri Joseph, Shamar Joseph, Vitel Lawes, Gudakesh Motie, Keemo Paul, Sherfane Rutherford, Jayden Seales.The T20I squad also features Hope, Roston Chase, Hetmyer, Akeal Hosein, Rovman Powell, Sherfane Rutherford, Romario Shepherd and Shamar Springer."We are looking to build on the momentum from our series win against Sri Lanka, with the long-term goal of developing a strong core of players ahead of the next T20 World Cup," Sammy said.The West Indies squad will leave the Caribbean on September 21 and reach Thiruvananthapuram on September 23, four days before the ODI series begins.West Indies T20I squad: Shai Hope (captain), Jewel Andrew, Roston Chase, Matthew Forde, Shimron Hetmyer, Akeal Hosein, Shamar Joseph, Gudakesh Motie, Keemo Paul, Kamil Pooran, Rovman Powell, Sherfane Rutherford, Quentin Sampson, Romario Shepherd, Shamar Springer.

Article Title: England sweep Sri Lanka 3-0, replace India at top of T20I rankings
Article Text:
Image credit: England Cricket

Buttler leads easy chase

Brook, Asalanka reflect on series

England beat Sri Lanka by eight wickets in the third T20I at Old Trafford in Manchester on Saturday to complete a 3-0 series sweep.The hosts chased down Sri Lanka's 125-run target with 62 balls to spare. The win also helped England move back to the top of the T20 world rankings, replacing India.It was England's 15th straight T20 win over Sri Lanka.Sri Lanka were bowled out for 124 with seven balls left in their innings.Pathum Nissanka top-scored with 36 off 24 balls, while Kamindu Mendis made 35 off 28. Will Jacks, Jofra Archer and Player of the Match Sonny Baker took two wickets each for England.England lost opener Aneurin Donald for 13, but Jos Buttler and Harry Brook quickly took control.Buttler smashed an unbeaten 62 off 32 balls, while Brook made 33. England reached 126-2 in just 9.4 overs.Buttler had earlier become the first batter to score 15,000 career T20 runs on Thursday.Brook finished as the highest run-scorer and was named Player of the Series."I think everybody stepped up in this series," said Brook. "Every game has been slightly different and we're playing the conditions extremely well."Sri Lanka's bowling also struggled, giving away nine wides, including two that went for four.Sri Lanka captain Charith Asalanka called the series a major disappointment for his team."A very disappointing series for us in both the major departments, batting and bowling... this is an important eye-opener for us of where we stand right now in T20 cricket comparing to the best teams in the world," said Asalanka."This is a time to get together as players, support staff, and our Sri Lanka cricket board as well to find solutions for these T20 problems. These are the best 15 players right now so we have to find solutions in the right way."England had won the first T20I in Southampton by 119 runs, with Brook scoring an unbeaten 114.England will next face Sri Lanka in three ODIs, starting at Durham's Chester-le-Street on Tuesday.
Article Summary: England beat Sri Lanka by eight wickets in the third T20I at Old Trafford. Hosts chased down Sri Lanka's 125-run target with 62 balls to spare. England move back to the top of the T20 world rankings, replacing India.

Article Title: ‘Only expectation from Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli is to keep scoring runs’: Aakash Chopra ahead of West Indies ODIs
Article Text:
Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli (ANI Photo)

‘They’ll score runs, win you matches’

Jaiswal-Gaikwad reserve battle, Pant’s white-ball future

NEW DELHI: With the 2027 ODI World Cup now just over a year away, former India batter Aakash Chopra believes Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli do not need to prove anything beyond what they have already done — they simply need to keep scoring runs.Rohit and Kohli are set to return to India’s ODI side for the three-match home series against the West Indies, beginning in Thiruvananthapuram on September 27. With Shubman Gill leading the side and KL Rahul named vice-captain, the experienced duo’s form will be one of the major talking points as India begin to shape their plans for the World Cup in South Africa.“The World Cup is just one year away now, and I know that if Rohit and Kohli get in, they will score runs, win you matches, and possibly win you trophies. So, looking at it from this perspective, the only expectation from Rohit and Kohli is just this: keep scoring runs,” Chopra told JioHotstar’s ‘Follow the Blues’.Both batters have remained productive in ODIs this year. Kohli has scored 384 runs in six innings at an average of 64.00 and a strike rate of over 106, with a century and three fifties.Rohit, meanwhile, has made 379 runs in nine innings at an average of 42.11 and a strike rate of over 99.His tally includes a century and a fifty, with his best score being 138 against England at Lord’s.For Chopra, their experience could become particularly valuable as India move towards the next World Cup.Rohit and Kohli are part of the 15-member squad for the West Indies ODIs alongside Ruturaj Gaikwad , Yashasvi Jaiswal and KL Rahul. Shreyas Iyer , who has been part of India’s recent ODI plans, is unavailable as he leads the Asian Games campaign.Chopra also backed the selectors’ overall composition of the squad, including the decision to bring in Dhruv Jurel as the second wicketkeeper.“With the available players, you try and make the most of what you have. The biggest change you notice is that KL Rahul has been made vice-captain in place of Shreyas Iyer because Shreyas Iyer will be at the Asian Games. There was certainly a question mark over Rishabh Pant , but I also liked Dhruv Jurel’s selection. So, considering all of that, a very good team has been picked, and full marks to the Indian team selectors,” he said.Chopra also identified a potential battle between Jaiswal and Gaikwad for a reserve batting spot ahead of the 2027 World Cup.“You have to think about who you can take along as reserves for the World Cup. So, there will be a toss-up here between Yashasvi Jaiswal and Ruturaj Gaikwad, who are both part of this team, and whenever they have played, they have scored a lot of runs. So, I am looking at an opportunity opening up for one of these two. Auqib Nabi (maiden ODI call-up for West Indies series) has been travelling with the team for some time now, but is not getting a chance to play in the XI. If he gets his opportunity, I will be quite excited to see him perform.”Chopra also spoke about Rishabh Pant’s omission from the ODI squad, despite his continued importance in the longer format.“Rishabh Pant is a very strange and very unique case. While he is playing Test cricket and is a very important member of the red-ball side, he was stripped of his vice-captaincy duties there as well. But in ODI cricket, without playing, he has been bid goodbye. At the same time, he has been made the captain of the Rest of India (ROI), which also tells you that, with respect to red-ball cricket, they are very serious about Rishabh playing a huge role in the longer format. But for white-ball cricket, as of now, I think this selection committee has made up its mind,” he said.The series will also provide an opportunity for Ravindra Jadeja and Nitish Kumar Reddy, with Chopra highlighting the competition for all-rounder spots ahead of the World Cup.“One big highlight, in my opinion, was pulling Nitish Kumar Reddy out of the Asian Games and playing him here. So, if Hardik Pandya is not available someday, they really want somebody who can bowl pace and bat as well. Ravindra Jadeja will have to, of course, take wickets and score runs. Fielding has always been his strong suit. But from a World Cup point of view, you have Axar Patel, Ravindra Jadeja, and Washington Sundar , and not all of them will go to South Africa. So, someone will be left out, and therefore, every time you get an opportunity, you have to grab it with both hands,” he said.India face the West Indies in the second ODI in Guwahati on September 30 before the series concludes in Chandigarh on October 3.
Article Summary: Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli are set to return to India’s ODI side for the three-match home series against the West Indies. Former India batter Aakash Chopra believes they do not need to prove anything beyond what they have already done. Chopra also identified a potential battle between Jaiswal and Gaikwad for a reserve batting spot ahead of the 2027 World Cup.

Article Title: ‘Main jhooth nahi bolunga’: Rohit Sharma reveals the comfort food he craved during sleepless Test-match nights
Article Text:

‘Nervousness mein mujhe neend nahi aati thi’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

His mother's homemade midnight snack

NEW DELHI: Former India captain Rohit Sharma has revealed the unlikely comfort food he would turn to during sleepless nights in the middle of Test matches, recalling how the pressure of his favourite format often left him nervous and craving a late-night snack.Rohit, who played 67 Tests for India between 2013 and 2024, opened up about his midnight cravings on his television show, ‘Family Full House with Rohit Sharma’. He revealed that his mother's homemade banana wafers became his go-to comfort food during those long nights on Test match duty.“Haan, hoti toh hai. Main jhooth nahi bolunga, lekin jab bhi main Test match khelta tha, andar bahut nervousness hoti thi. Toh Test match ke time khaas karke, kyunki yeh mera favourite format tha, Test match khelna,” Rohit said.The former opener called time on his Test career last year after scoring 4,301 runs in 67 matches at an average of 40.57, including 12 centuries and 18 fifties. His highest score in the format was 212.Rohit explained that the demands of Test cricket often made it difficult for him to switch off after a day's play.“Kyunki Test match khelna aasaan format nahi hai. Koi bhi format aasaan nahi hota, lekin Test match ke apne alag-alag challenges hote the.Toh Test match ke liye main hamesha nervous rehta tha aur nervousness mein mujhe neend nahi aati thi, toh raat bhar main jaaga rehta tha,” he said.Those sleepless nights, in turn, often brought with them the urge to eat something.“Toh aap jaage rehte ho toh kuch na kuch khaane ka mann karta tha. Toh main hamesha mere saath mera comfort food rakhta tha, jo meri mummy hamesha bana ke deti thi, woh tha banana wafers,” Rohit said.The snack came with a personal touch. Rohit revealed that the banana wafers were made by his mother, who used a baking method rather than frying them.“Woh fried nahi hota tha. Meri mummy ke kuch tareeke the, woh bake karti thi usko aur woh main hamesha apne saath leke chalta tha. Toh kabhi bhi mann karta tha toh usse kha leta tha,” he said.For a batter who spent years dealing with the mental and physical demands of the longest format, the simple homemade snack offered a familiar taste of home during the intensity of Test cricket.
Article Summary: Rohit revealed his mother's homemade banana wafers became his go-to comfort food during those long nights on Test match duty. The former opener called time on his Test career last year after scoring 4,301 runs in 67 matches at an average of 40.57. His highest score in the format was 212.

Pat Cummins has faced some of India's biggest cricketing names during his international career, but when asked to identify the toughest Indian opponent he has come up against, the Australia captain did not pick MS Dhoni Virat Kohli or Rohit Sharma.Instead, Cummins went back to the player who repeatedly tested Australia's patience during two memorable Border-Gavaskar Trophy series and chose Cheteshwar Pujara as his toughest Indian opponent.The Australia Test and ODI captain made the admission in a recent promotional video for Prime Video Sport, where he was asked to name the toughest player he had faced from India, Pakistan, New Zealand, England, Sri Lanka, South Africa and the West Indies.For India, there was little hesitation in his choice.“India, I'm going to say, Pujara. Really hard to get out. Just like death by a thousand papercuts. Happy to face 100 dot balls if he wanted to. Not going to give you a chance,” said Cummins in a video shared on social media.Pujara's reputation as an immovable presence at the crease was particularly evident against Australia. He played 25 Tests against them and accumulated 2,074 runs at an average of 49.38.Nearly half of those runs, 993, came in Australia, where Pujara struck three centuries and five fifties. His highest score Down Under was 193.The 2018-19 and 2020-21 Border-Gavaskar Trophy series remain synonymous with Pujara's determined resistance against Australia's pace attack, including Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood.Pujara retired from international cricket last year after a career spanning 103 Tests for India. He finished with 7,195 runs at an average of 43.6, including 19 centuries and 35 fifties.Cummins selected Brendon McCullum as his toughest opponent from New Zealand, recalling the former New Zealand captain's aggressive approach at the top of the order.“From New Zealand, I played Brendon McCullum a couple of times when he was really going hard at the top of the order," said Cummins.For Pakistan, Cummins opted for former spinner Saeed Ajmal, “Pakistan, Saeed Ajmal. It was like the last ball of the over; I walked in, Saeed Ajmal just goes, and I went, what? Clean bowled. I have never seen anything like that," Cummins said.His selections from the remaining countries were equally notable. Sir Alastair Cook was his choice from England, AB de Villiers from South Africa, Tillakaratne Dilshan from Sri Lanka and Chris Gayle from the West Indies.
Article Summary: Pat Cummins named Cheteshwar Pujara as his toughest Indian Test opponent. Cummins made the admission in a recent promotional video for Prime Video Sport. The Australia Test and ODI captain also named Brendon McCullum as the toughest opponent from New Zealand. Sir Alastair Cook was his choice from England.

Article Title: ‘Both trophies will come’: BCCI’s big update on Asia Cup trophies India refused to take from Naqvi
Article Text:
Indian women's cricket team and Mohsin Naqvi

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Asia Cup trophies won by India's men's and women's teams remain in Dubai, but BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia has assured that both pieces of silverware will eventually make their way to the board's headquarters in Mumbai.Saikia confirmed the development after the BCCI's 95th Annual General Meeting in Mumbai on Friday, although he stopped short of specifying when the trophies would arrive. The men's and women's teams had both declined to receive the Asia Cup trophy from Asian Cricket Council president Mohsin Naqvi, leaving the silverware at the ACC headquarters in Dubai."Asia Cup trophies, we hope it will come one day," Saikia said in Mumbai on Friday after the BCCI's 95th Annual General Meeting.“I will not give you a timeline, but I can assure you that both the trophies will come up and land up in this BCCI head office at the Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai,” he added.The latest development follows India's women's team refusing to attend the trophy presentation after beating Sri Lanka in the Women's T20 Asia Cup final last week. Harmanpreet Kaur 's side did not appear at the presentation ceremony with Naqvi on the dais, while a similar situation had unfolded after India's men's team won the Asia Cup last year.The women's team instead conducted its own medal presentation after the final, with BCCI secretary Saikia and vice-president Rajeev Shukla presenting Nandni Sharma with the fielding medal. The official ceremony later saw Naqvi present the runners-up cheque to Sri Lanka.Saikia had already made the BCCI's position clear a day after the women's final, describing the decision not to accept the trophy from Naqvi as a "firm institutional decision".“Our position had been communicated to the ACC in advance that the Indian team would not participate in the trophy presentation under the circumstances. Given the circumstances and the sentiments prevailing in the country, the BCCI felt that it would not be appropriate for the team to receive the trophy in the proposed manner,” Saikia told news agency PTI.“This was a firm institutional decision, reflective of the position we have maintained, and was not directed at the players, the tournament or the sport,” he added.The issue could have implications beyond the Asia Cup, with India and Pakistan both competing at the Asian Games in Japan. The Asian Games cricket tournament is being conducted under the ACC, while both Indian teams are among the contenders for gold. The possibility of Naqvi being involved in a medal presentation could therefore become another point of attention.Saikia's latest comments also come with Naqvi's current term as ACC president approaching its scheduled conclusion in April 2027. Whether he receives an extension will depend on the support of ACC members.The strained cricketing relationship between India and Pakistan has remained evident since the Pahalgam terror attack, with players from the two teams having refused to shake hands with each other in subsequent encounters.
Article Summary: India's men's and women's cricket teams refuse to accept Asia Cup trophies. Asian Cricket Council president Mohsin Naqvi left the silverware in Dubai. But BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia says the trophies will eventually arrive in Mumbai. It follows India's women's team refusing to attend the trophy presentation.

Article Title: 'There are very few people from Keralam in this sport': Vidarsa K Vinod after becoming the state's first Asian Games shooting medallist

From NCC to Asian Games medal

Vidarsa K Vinod has created history by becoming the first woman sportsperson from Kerala to win an Asian Games medal in shooting. Vidarsa won silver in the women’s 10m air rifle team event at the Asian Games in Japan, marking a memorable debut at the continental event.For her, the medal is especially meaningful because she is also competing in the women’s 50m rifle 3 Positions event, which she considers her main event.Speaking to a TV channel, she said she was delighted to win a medal in her first Asian Games."There are very few people from Keralam in this sport and I am happy to be first woman from the state to win a medal in shooting," she said.Vidarsa took up shooting in 2018 through the National Cadet Corps (NCC) and decided to make it her profession the following year. Much of her training has been based in Delhi as she worked her way into the international circuit.Her journey has also involved personal sacrifices. Vinod got married around a year and a half ago, but soon after the wedding, she resumed training and began competing in international events, leaving little time for her and her husband to be together.She credited her medal to the backing she received from her family and coach."Without any of their support I could not have achieved this," she said.Her mother said the family was extremely proud of the achievement."I am proud of her achievement," she said.Her father, meanwhile, hopes his daughter can go one step further and win gold in her main event.The 10m air rifle team silver has already given Vinod renewed confidence ahead of the 50m rifle 3 Positions event on September 26.She also welcomed the Kerala government's decision to announce cash rewards for Asian Games medallists. The state has promised Rs 50 lakh for gold, Rs 30 lakh for silver and Rs 20 lakh for bronze."Prior to this our sportspersons had not received any such cash prize from the government. So, this support gives us energy to perform," she said.
